newsitem.title: CHINA: China mulls diesel import limit to up retail price.
newsitem.headline: China mulls diesel import limit to up retail price.

text.p: China is considering limiting diesel imports outside state quotas to try to reverse a slump in retail prices, oil officials said on Thursday.
Senior oil officials were meeting in Beijing to decide whether to limit diesel imports through informal measures to boost retail prices, said one oil trader who declined to be identified.
Falling international prices, huge imports and rising domestic stockpiles have caused China's retail diesel prices to drop sharply in the first half of 1997, traders said.
In some areas, retail prices are below refinery selling prices, making it impossible for refiners to cover their costs.
Traders in Hong Kong said that in Guangdong, in southern China, retail diesel prices were just over 2,000 yuan per tonne and in Shanghai they were 1,955 yuan on Thursday.
This compared with the official ex-refinery selling price of 2,190 yuan.
Diesel prices have partly fallen because of surging imports, which in the year to the end of April totalled 2.4 million tonnes, or 77 percent up on a year earlier.

China entrusts diesel imports under quotas to only three state-owned oil companies -- China National Petrochemical Corporation (SINOPEC), China National Chemical Import and Export Corporation and China National United Oil Corporation.
However, imports by other organisations, mainly in China's southern provinces of Fujian and Guangdong have upset the domestic market, an oil trader said.
"If the state could limit imports, I think domestic diesel prices would rise," he said, without elaborating.
However, China was unlikely to cut the ex-refinery price of diesel despite declining domestic and international retail prices, officials said.
Beijing had raised the official ex-refinery price of diesel twice in the fourth quarter of 1996 to try to stimulate domestic output.
"We have not considered a price adjustment recently," said an official of the Price Administration department of the State Planning Commission.
"It is impossible to cut oil prices," said an official of the China National United Oil Corporation.
Refinery sources said that the current official ex-refinery price was just sufficient to cover costs, so a cut would be difficult to handle.

But the official said domestic prices of crude oil were likely to rise because the government planned to free domestic crude prices within the next couple of years, allowing state-controlled prices to float at international market levels, the official said.
"Oil product prices should also rise, following the crude prices," the official said, adding that cutting prices of oil products would hit profits of already squeezed domestic refineries.
